citeAs: Krishna, R., Zhu, Y., Groth, O., Johnson, J., Hata, K., Kravitz, J., Chen, S., Kalantidis, Y., Li, L.-J., Shamma, D. A., Bernstein, M. S., and Fei-Fei, L. (2016). Visual Genome: Connecting Language and Vision Using Crowdsourced Dense Image Annotations. arXiv:1602.07332.
creator: Ranjay Krishna, Yuke Zhu, Oliver Groth, Justin Johnson, Kenji Hata, Joshua Kravitz, Stephanie Chen, Yannis Kalantidis, Li-Jia Li, David A. Shamma, Michael S. Bernstein, Li Fei-Fei (Stanford University, Dresden University of Technology, Yahoo Inc., Snapchat Inc.)
description: Visual Genome is a large-scale dataset of over 108K images densely annotated with region descriptions, objects, attributes, relationships, region graphs, scene graphs, and question-answer pairs. Each image has an average of 21 objects, 18 attributes, and 18 pairwise relationships between objects, with all concepts canonicalized to WordNet synsets. The dataset contains over 4 million objects, 1.6 million attributes, 1.8 million relationships, and 1.7 million question-answer pairs, designed to enable cognitive computer vision tasks such as image description and visual question answering.
name: Visual Genome
rai:annotationsPerItem: Each image has an average of 42 region descriptions, 21 objects, 16 attributes, 18 relationships, and 17 question-answer pairs. For verification, each annotation is reviewed by 3 unique workers.
rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 33,000 unique workers contributed. Geographic distribution: 93.02% from the United States, 1.29% Philippines, 1.13% Kenya, 0.94% India, 0.50% Russia, 0.47% Canada, 2.65% others. Age range: 18 to 68 years old, with the majority between 25 and 34 years old. Gender: 54.15% male and 45.85% female.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Canonicalization precision and recall were evaluated on held-out test sets of 200 randomly sampled items: Objects: 88.0% precision, 98.5% recall; Attributes: 85.7% precision, 95.9% recall; Relationships: 92.9% precision, 88.5% recall. The dataset achieved a 94.1% worker retention rate. BLEU score thresholds of 0.7 were used to enforce diversity in region descriptions.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Workers were asked to draw bounding boxes and write region descriptions, extract objects/attributes/relationships, and create question-answer pairs. For region descriptions, workers wrote 3 descriptions per HIT, with BLEU score thresholds (0.7) enforcing diversity. For objects, workers extracted nouns and drew tight bounding boxes satisfying coverage and quality requirements. For QAs, workers followed three rules: start with one of the seven Ws, avoid ambiguous questions, and be precise. All annotations went through a verification stage using majority voting (3 workers, 2/3 agreement required) or rapid judgments for objects.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset is somewhat biased towards images of people, as the top synsets show. There is also a bias towards sports images (ski, ballplayer, racket are the top synsets). Certain sports (skiing, surfboarding) are overrepresented in attribute descriptions due to a bias towards these sports in the image set. 93.02% of annotators were from the United States, which may introduce cultural bias in annotations.
rai:dataCollection: Visual Genome was collected entirely by crowd workers from Amazon Mechanical Turk. The dataset was collected over the course of 6 months after 15 months of experimentation and iteration on the data representation. Approximately 800,000 Human Intelligence Tasks (HITs) were launched on AMT, where each HIT involved creating descriptions, questions and answers, or region graphs. Workers were paid between $6-$8 per hour. The pipeline involved multiple stages: region descriptions, object extraction, attribute/relationship extraction, scene graph construction, and question-answer collection, each with verification steps.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The dataset uses 108,249 images from the intersection of MS-COCO (328,000 images) and YFCC100M (100 million images). These are real-world, non-iconic images uploaded to Flickr by users, ranging from 72 pixels wide to 1280 pixels wide, with an average width of 500 pixels.
rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: The dataset was collected over the course of 6 months after 15 months of experimentation and iteration on the data representation.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping, User-generated content data
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Scene graphs were constructed by merging region graphs: objects from different region graphs were merged if their bounding boxes had an intersection over union of 0.8 or higher. Workers confirmed merges for objects with significant overlap. For QA experiments, data was split 60% training and 40% test. For attribute/relationship experiments, 80% training, 10% validation, 10% test splits were used, with random sampling of 500 instances per category for balance.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: All objects, attributes, relationships, and noun phrases were canonicalized to WordNet synsets using Stanford NLP tools for noun phrase extraction, mapped to most frequent matching synsets, with hand-crafted rules for common failure cases (30 rules for objects, 15 for attributes, 20 for relationships). Attributes were normalized by morphology (stemming). Workers verified canonicalization mappings on AMT. For region descriptions, BLEU score thresholds (0.7) were used to enforce diversity. Objects were co-referenced across region descriptions using intersection-over-union threshold of 0.8.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to advance cognitive computer vision capabilities, enabling applications such as image search, question answering, and robotic interactions. It provides a comprehensive knowledge representation for visual understanding that could benefit AI systems requiring deeper scene understanding beyond simple object recognition.
rai:dataUseCases: Training and benchmarking computer vision models for cognitive scene understanding tasks including: image description/captioning, visual question answering, object detection, attribute prediction, relationship prediction, dense image captioning, semantic image retrieval, scene graph generation, knowledge representation, and action recognition.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Stanford's dependency parser (Manning et al., 2014) was used to automatically extract nouns from region descriptions as suggestions for workers. Stanford NLP tools were used to extract noun phrases for canonicalization. BLEU score computation was used programmatically to enforce description diversity.

evidence.name: In this paper, we present the Visual Genome dataset to enable the modeling of such relationships.
evidence.description: our dataset contains over 100K images where each image has an average of 21 objects, 18 attributes, and 18 pairwise relationships between objects. We canonicalize the objects, attributes, relationships, and noun phrases in region descriptions and questions answer pairs to WordNet synsets. Together, these annotations represent the densest and largest dataset of image descriptions, objects, attributes, relationships, and question answers.

evidence.inLanguage: All the descriptions and QAs that we collect are freeform worker-generated texts. They are not constrained by any limitations. For example, we do not force workers to refer to a man in the image as a man.

evidence.isLiveDataset: The first release of the Visual Genome dataset uses 108,249 images from the intersection of the YFCC100M (Thomee et al., 2016) and MS-COCO (Lin et al., 2014).
evidence.rai:dataCollection: Visual Genome was collected and verified entirely by crowd workers from Amazon Mechanical Turk. In this section, we outline the pipeline employed in creating all the components of the dataset. Each component (region descriptions, objects, attributes, relationships, region graphs, scene graphs, questions and answers) involved multiple task stages.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionType: Visual Genome was collected and verified entirely by crowd workers from Amazon Mechanical Turk. The Visual Genome dataset consists of all 108,249 images from the intersection of MS-COCO's (Lin et al., 2014) 328,000 images and YFCC's (Thomee et al., 2016) 100 million images. These images are real-world, non-iconic images that were uploaded onto Flickr by users.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The Visual Genome dataset consists of all 108,249 images from the intersection of MS-COCO's (Lin et al., 2014) 328,000 images and YFCC's (Thomee et al., 2016) 100 million images. These images are real-world, non-iconic images that were uploaded onto Flickr by users. The images range from as small as 72 pixels wide to as large as 1280 pixels wide, with an average width of 500 pixels.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: The dataset was collected over the course of 6 months after 15 months of experimentation and iteration on the data representation.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: We used Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) as our primary source of annotations. Overall, a total of over 33,000 unique workers contributed to the dataset.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Verification is conducted using two separate strategies: majority voting (Snow et al., 2008) and rapid judgments (Krishna et al., 2016). All components of the dataset except objects are verified using majority voting. Majority voting (Snow et al., 2008) involves three unique workers looking at each annotation and voting on whether it is factually correct. An annotation is added to our dataset if at least two (a majority) out of the three workers verify that it is correct.
evidence.rai:annotatorDemographics: 93.02% of workers contributed from the United States. The majority of our workers were between the ages of 25 and 34 years old. Our youngest contributor was 18 years old and the oldest was 68 years old. We also had a near-balanced split of 54.15% male and 45.85% female workers.
evidence.rai:annotationsPerItem: Our dataset contains on average a total of 42 region descriptions per image. Each image in our dataset consists of an average of 21 objects. On average, each image in Visual Genome contains 21 attributes. On average, each image in our dataset contains 18 relationships. On average, every image has 17 QA pairs.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Precision Recall Objects 88.0 98.5 Attributes 85.7 95.9 Relationships 92.9 88.5 Table 5: Precision, recall, and mapping accuracy percentages for object, attribute, and relationship canonicalization.
evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: We use the Stanford NLP tools (Manning et al., 2014) to extract the noun phrases from the region descriptions and QAs. Next, we map them to their most frequent matching synset in WordNet according to WordNet lexeme counts. We then refine this simple heuristic by hand-crafting mapping rules for the 30 most common failure cases.
evidence.rai:machineAnnotationTools: we also use Stanford's dependency parser (Manning et al., 2014) to extract nouns automatically and send them to the workers as suggestions. While the parser manages to find most of the nouns, it sometimes misses compound nouns, so we avoided completely depending on this automated method.
evidence.rai:dataBiases: Our dataset is somewhat biased towards images of people, as Figure 13 shows; however, they are quite diverse overall, as the top 25 synsets each have over 800 images, while the top 50 synsets each have over 500 examples. Certain sports (skiing, surfboarding) are overrepresented due to a bias towards these sports in our images.
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: In this paper, we introduce the Visual Genome dataset with the aim of training and benchmarking the next generation of computer models for comprehensive scene understanding. Understanding scenes would enable important applications such as image search, question answering, and robotic interactions.
evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: Understanding scenes would enable important applications such as image search, question answering, and robotic interactions. Visual Genome is a large formalized knowledge representation for visual understanding and a more complete set of descriptions and question answers that grounds visual concepts to language.
evidence.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: We say that objects from different graphs refer to the same object if their bounding boxes have an overlap over union of 0.8. However, this heuristic might contain false positives. So, before merging two objects, we ask workers to confirm that a pair of objects with significant overlap are indeed the same object.
